tip: Παντρεύονται (pandrévonde) looks passive but means plain 'they marry'. Some verbs exist only in this -ομαι (-ome) family, and marrying is one of them.
Ερωτευμένη (erotevméni) = in love, with the -η (-i) ending because a woman is speaking; a man says ερωτευμένος (erotevménos).
Σκέφτομαι να (skéftome na) = think of doing. Greek links the two verbs with να (na), since there is no plain 'to tell' form to fall back on.
Short object words come before the verb: μας σύστησαν (mas sístisan) = literally 'us they-introduced'. In statements they normally sit ahead of the verb.
Μαλώνουν (malónun) = they argue, from μαλώνω (malóno), which also means 'to scold' when it takes an object.
Μεταξύ τους (metaksí tus) is literally 'between them' and does the work of 'each other': μοιάζουν πολύ μεταξύ τους (miázun polí metaksí tus) = they look a lot alike.
Μοιάζω (miázo) takes σε (se = to) rather than a plain object: μοιάζει στον παππού (miázi ston papú) = she takes after her grandfather.
Δεν αντέχω (dhen andékho) = I can't bear it, stronger than δεν μπορώ (dhen boró), the plain 'I can't'; it is about endurance running out.
Δεμένη (dheméni) is literally 'tied', from δένω (dhéno = to tie): δεμένη οικογένεια (dheméni ikoyénia) = a close-knit family.
The τα (ta) in τα πάει καλά (ta pái kalá) = 'gets along' points at nothing – it's a built-in dummy 'them', shared by several Greek idioms.
Το παίρνω στραβά (to pérno stravá) = to take it the wrong way; στραβά (stravá) on its own means crookedly.
Ας τα βρούμε (as ta vrúme) is literally 'let's find them' = let's make up. The τα (ta) refers to nothing specific, another idiom built on a dummy 'them'.
Αξίζει να (aksízi na) plus a verb = it's worth doing: αξίζει να δώσουμε (aksízi na dhósume) = it's worth giving, with no word for 'it' needed.
Δίνω το χέρι (dhíno to khéri) = to shake hands or make up: έδωσα το χέρι μου (édhosa to khéri mu) = I offered my hand.
Φοβήθηκα (fovíthika) looks passive but just means 'I got scared'. Many feeling verbs take this -θηκα (-thika) past: λυπήθηκα (lipíthika) = I felt sad.
English is interested in something; Greek is interested for it: ενδιαφέρομαι για (endhiaférome ya) = I care about. The για (ya) is fixed with this verb.
Χαιρόμουν (kherómun) is the ongoing past: I was glad, again and again. It pairs naturally with κάθε φορά (káthe forá) = every time, since repetition normally takes this form.
The verb agrees with the thing liked: το ρεμπέτικο (to rebétiko) is one thing, so μου αρέσει (mu arési) stays singular – 'it pleases me'.
Λαϊκά (la-i-ká) = popular folk songs, and the two dots split the vowels, so you say it in three syllables: la-i-ká.
Έντεχνη (éndekhni) = 'art' or refined, and έντεχνη μουσική (éndekhni musikí) names a whole Greek genre of literary songwriting, roughly 'refined pop'.
Της τραγουδίστριας (tis traghudhístrias) = of the singer, a woman: the -ίστρια (-ístria) ending marks the feminine, next to τραγουδιστής (traghudhistís) for a man.
Γλέντι (ghléndi) = a feast with music and dancing, the word for a proper night out rather than a quiet dinner.
Ζεϊμπέκικο (ze-i-békiko) = a solo, improvised dance, traditionally a man's and a staple of rebetiko music.
Liking many things makes the verb plural: τα τραγούδια (ta traghúdhia) are plural, so it's μου αρέσουν (mu arésun) – 'they please me'.
Σιγοτραγουδάω (sighotraghudháo) = to hum, literally 'sing softly': σιγο- (sigho- = softly) glued onto τραγουδάω (traghudháo = I sing).
Ανεβάζω (anevázo) means 'raise', and online it means upload or release: ανεβάζει νέο τραγούδι (anevázi néo traghúdhi) = drops a new song.
Κομμάτι (komáti) = a track of music, and also just 'a piece' of anything: ένα κομμάτι ψωμί (éna komáti psomí) = a piece of bread.
Θερινό σινεμά (therinó sinemá) is literally 'summer cinema' = the open-air screens that run all summer in Greece, a normal part of the season.
Κόσμος (kósmos) means both 'world' and 'people': γεμάτος κόσμο (yemátos kósmo) is literally 'full of world', the normal Greek way to say packed.
Παρακολουθήσαμε (parakoluthísame) comes from παρακολουθώ (parakoluthó = watch/follow), the verb for shows and documentaries and a step more formal than βλέπω (vlépo).
